transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-04
Start: 10:00 PST
Duration: ~49 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Singh (Redwood SE), Jules Park (Redwood Support); Leah Torres (CTO), Marcus Bell (Backend Eng), Priya Sharma (SRE) - Cinder Analytics
Shared artifacts: https://redwood.app/s/ff/configs/rampflow-tuned-20261206.json, shared sheet: https://docs.company/xr2 - (note: shortened link)

Summary: Quick health check on week-3 tuning. Reviewed steady-state 2h run, discussed queue jitter, suggested concurrency buckets and continuous-batching policy tweaks. Agreed on 24h steady-state validation and a short benchmark on dedicated capacity next week.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. quick check — we only have 50 minutes, so we'll do a quick recap then dive into the tuning notes. is that still ok for folks?
[00:14] Leah Torres: yes, that's perfect. we got the 2 hour exports, and Marcus got me up to speed. plenty to go through.
[00:22] Marcus Bell: yep, uploaded the p90/p99 histograms and the qps traces around the spike periods, you'll see the midday burst pattern.
[00:30] Omar Singh: cool, i pulled the logs. first pass, the KV cache hit rate is about 28% which is lower than we expected given the prompt preambles — looks like prefix variance is the culprit.
[00:45] Leah Torres: hm, prefix variance meaning users drop in with slightly different system prompts?
[00:51] Omar Singh: yeah and also a lot of dynamic JSON fields in the prompt that prevent prefix reuse. we can either do stronger prompt normalization or tune the continuous-batching window to increase merge opportunities. tradeoff is latency vs token cost.
[01:05] Marcus Bell: our product requirement is 200ms p95 for inference in the interactive flow, but we can accept 350ms p95 for batched background jobs. clarifying that because it affects recommended concurrency.
[01:18] Maya Chen: good, that helps. our suggestion for this week was three candidate concurrency buckets: conserv (8), balanced (16), and aggressive (24). Omar, can you walk through the expected latency curves?
[01:30] Omar Singh: sure. optimistic note: with continuous batching tuned to a 25ms batching window and KV cache warmed, conserv gives ~180ms p95, balanced ~240ms, aggressive ~310ms — but aggressive brings token unit cost down ~22%. there's jitter risk if qps spikes beyond provisioning and queue depth climbs.
[01:58] Leah Torres: where does dedicated vs hosted come into play? we spoke earlier about starting hosted but moving to dedicated if we hit steady ramp.
[02:06] Maya Chen: correct. hosted lets you ramp without infra ops; dedicated gives more headroom for concurrency and lower jitter, but requires the reserved capacity commit. for this POC we can run a short dedicated benchmark to quantify the delta.
[02:20] Priya Sharma: we also need to consider network egress and TLS handshakes inside our VPC. during the 2h run p99 we saw occasional 800-1200ms outliers which tracked to peering flaps on our side.
[02:33] Omar Singh: yes those are infra noise — we filtered those traces in the analysis but they do affect perception. if Priya can confirm a maintenance window for peering test we can re-run.
[02:45] Marcus Bell: note, a chunk of those outliers were correlated with bursters hitting long prompt lengths — so sequence length skew is a factor.
[02:55] Maya Chen: ok -- quick recap of tuning changes we pushed this week: 1) reduced batching window from 40ms to 25ms during interactive mode, 2) enabled adaptive concurrency backoff at 95th queue depth threshold, 3) added a sample prompt-normalizer to improve KV cache reuse. did customers see these changes land?
[03:20] Marcus Bell: yes, we tested the branch on staging. p95 improved but we still have mid-tier jitter.
[03:28] Leah Torres: when you say adaptive concurrency backoff, what are the trigger thresholds?
[03:33] Jules Park: (Support) we set a soft queue depth threshold at 120 requests in-flight for a single pod; above that it reduces concurrency by 25% over 10s. it's meant to avoid long tail amplification.
[03:45] Priya Sharma: that seems reasonable. what's the mechanism for pod scale? is it k8s HPA or Redwood autoscaler?
[03:51] Omar Singh: Redwood autoscaler for Dedicated; for Hosted it's our managed scheduler. both can scale but HPA is not in the loop for the short-window continous-batching decisions.
[04:05] Marcus Bell: any config we need to change in our deployment to allow the autoscaler to make good decisions?
[04:10] Maya Chen: we'll share a recommended HPA-ish set of metrics but mostly the server side needs to see the qps histogram and the request timestamp distribution — Marcus, you already uploaded the histogram but can you include a sample per-minute breakdown?
[04:22] Marcus Bell: yes, i'll add that.
[04:25] [05:10] (skipping forward — middle section contains detailed debug logs and reference to the shared replay)
[05:12] Omar Singh: i want to call out something subtle: continuous batching helps when request arrival is Poisson-ish; when you have tightly correlated bursts (like many users hitting a nightly job at the same second) batching yields large queues and longer tail latencies. for those patterns, we recommended admission control + burst smoothing token bucket on the client side.
[05:35] Leah Torres: admission control on the client side is doable, we have a gateway that can do rate shaping. what's the recommended smoothing window?
[05:40] Omar Singh: based on your traces 2-5s smoothing would flatten the peaks enough to preserve batching benefits but keep interactive latency sensible.
[05:50] Priya Sharma: curious — how much cost do we save by moving from balanced to aggressive concurrency if we keep latency at acceptable levels?
[05:57] Omar Singh: rough calc from your run: going from balanced (16) to aggressive (24) drops per-token CPU time by ~18-22% at steady-state because batching utilization improves. however, if queueing increases p95 beyond your threshold, user experience suffers. so it's a business-decisions tradeoff.
[06:15] Maya Chen: we proposed a hybrid: keep interactive endpoints on balanced (16) with 25ms window; route background jobs to aggressive (24) during off-peak windows with longer batching windows and higher latency SLO.
[06:28] Marcus Bell: that fits product constraints — interactive must remain snappy. also we need to think about warmup latencies for cold cache after deploys.
[06:36] Omar Singh: warmup is real; suggested warmup is a lightweight synthetic traffic for 5-10 minutes after rollout to rebuild KV cache. we can provide a sample load-generator script in the repo.
[06:48] Leah Torres: do you have a sense of the expected cost delta if we do the warmup vs not?
[06:52] Omar Singh: negligible versus long tail costs — warmup might add 1-2% to daily token usage but prevents p99 spikes that are more costly in customer ops.
[07:05] Leah Torres: ok. next — security/compliance quick check, Priya?
[07:10] Priya Sharma: yes. we need the SOC2 artifacts and KMS integration docs. also we have an internal legal question about token retention for debug logs — can Redwood redact or truncate incoming prompts in logs?
[07:20] Jules Park: we support configurable retention and redaction rules; we can also redact full prompts at ingest and only save metadata for debugging. i'll attach the policy doc after the call.
[07:30] Priya Sharma: perfect. please also include the HSM/KMS flowchart.
[07:34] Jules Park: will do.
[07:36] [12:00] (discussion about sample replay results and where spike artifacts originate)
[12:30] Marcus Bell: i noticed one neural spike where the sequence length jumped from 80 to 320 tokens. is that a user action?
[12:36] Leah Torres: that was a bulk export triggered by a data analyst. we didn't expect it to go to inference but it did.
[12:42] Omar Singh: bulk exports like that need routing to a background queue with longer SLOs. otherwise they distort queues for interactive flows.
[12:51] Maya Chen: agreed — we'll supply a routing rule example in the config.
[12:55] Leah Torres: timeline wise, if we complete the 24h steady-state run and the dedicated benchmark, what's a reasonable go-live target?
[13:03] Maya Chen: if results look good, a staggered rollout in production branch within 3 weeks after positive benchmarks is typical. so earliest go-live target: 2027-01-05 assuming approvals.
[13:15] Priya Sharma: makes sense. legal and security reviews will likely add 1-2 weeks.
[13:20] Maya Chen: fine, we can parallelize security docs and the steady-state run.
[13:25] [30:00] (deep dive on tuning knobs — sample config excerpt read out)
[30:12] Omar Singh: reading sample config: continuous_batching: enabled, max_hold_ms: 25, adaptive_concurrency: {target_concurrency: 16, step_down_on_queue_depth: 0.95, backoff_pct: 0.25}, kvcache: {soft_ttl_ms: 120000, warmup_policy: synthetic_replay}. note: braces are shorthand in call notes, full json in repo link.
[30:40] Marcus Bell: will the adaptive_concurrency scheme cause oscillation? we saw some oscillatory patterns in the staging run.
[30:47] Omar Singh: possibly if the probe period is too short. we set a dampening window of 10s in the current policy; if you want more stability we can increase to 30s which slows reaction but reduces oscillation.
[30:58] Leah Torres: let's start with 10s dampening and observe in the 24h run; if it oscillates we'll bump to 30s.
[31:05] Maya Chen: agreed. any other blockers?
[31:08] Priya Sharma: firewall rules and peering — i'll confirm.
[31:12] Marcus Bell: i'll add per-minute histograms and a note about bulk export routes.
[31:17] Leah Torres: we'll run the 24h test starting 2026-12-07 and upload results by 2026-12-10.
[31:25] Maya Chen: perfect. final recap and owners?
[31:28] Maya Chen: Redwood to share tuned config and replay scripts by 2026-12-06 (Maya/Omar). Redwood to schedule 1hr dedicated benchmark with Marcus for week of 12/13. Customer to run 24h steady-state by 12/07 and upload metrics by 12/10. Priya to confirm peering and firewall rules by 12/08. Jules to attach SOC2/KMS docs by 12/07.
[31:55] Leah Torres: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[32:00] Maya Chen: thanks — we'll follow up in the shared thread.

(End of call)
